newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's economy to pick up gradually - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Spain's economy to pick up gradually - OECD.

text.p: Spain's economy will be sluggish near-term but growth should quicken to three percent in 1998, boosted by export competitiveness, corporate profitability and a gradual recovery in consumption, the OECD said on Thursday.

In its twice yearly report, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said the pickup in gross domestic product growth would be accompanied by employment gains, but the jobless rate would remain high at above 20 percent in 1998.

"The contradictory demand effect of substantial fiscal consolidation - with a general government fiscal deficit of three percent within reach in 1997 - should be mitigated by a cautious easing of monetary policy as inflation declines towards its medium-term target of below three percent in 1997," it said.
GDP would expand by 2.1 percent in 1996 and 2.6 percent in 1997, the Paris-based think tank said.
The chances for a strong recovery hinged on continued wage moderation, which would facilitate the easing of monetary policy and support employment growth, the OECD said.
It forecast that 1997 inflation, based on the private consumption deflator, would decline to 2.9 percent and then to 2.5 percent in 1998.
At the same time unemployment is likely to ease slightly to 22.4 percent in 1997 from 22.7 in 1996, and then improve to 21.7 percent in 1998.

But the OECD added that the government commitment to slash the public sector deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997, with a primary balance adjustment of about one percent of GDP, might restrict future economic growth.
"Output growth will be restrained for a time by the effects of the large fiscal adjustment that has ocurred in 1996 and is envisaged for 1997", the report said.

Lower interest rates should counterbalance tighter fiscal policy, despite the fact that the main uncertainty surrounding the projections concerns developments in wages and interest rates themselves, the report said.
Structural rigidities in the labour market and a pick-up in employment may place some upward pressure on wages, it noted.
Spanish fiscal correction was once again focused on discretionary spending -- notably wages, investment and public sector transfers and subsidies, the report said.
This would imply "once-off measures which will result in upward pressure on future budgets".

So while expectations about fiscal consolidation and structural reform have buoyed financial markets, the OECD concluded that "slippage in policy implementation might have negative consequences on interest rates".
